## Full read
Megan's notebook in Kenya starts with a shove among olive baboons, not with a grand theory. One animal crowds another at the edge of the troop. A quick reading says rank caused it. A slower reading asks what rank has been doing to stress, what stress has been doing to behavior, and how years of social life changed the odds before that shove happened.

That is why the method matters for good behavior too. The same kind of layered system that can produce cruelty can also produce restraint. Threat detection can make a person lash out, but it can also help them protect a child. Bonding can make care wider, but it can also make loyalty blind. The tool is not a moral eraser. It is a better map.

The full walk uses these clocks: one second; seconds to minutes; hours to days; days to months. Then it keeps going: adolescence and early development; genes; culture; evolution. Each clock asks a different question. What fired right before the act? What body state had been building? What did learning teach? What did the surrounding group reward? What did older history make easier to feel or do?

This is where simple arguments get slippery, usually while sounding satisfyingly stern. If you stop at the last second, you overpraise willpower and overblame failure. If you stop at childhood, you can make the present moment disappear. If you stop at genes or evolution, you can sound deep while doing the intellectual equivalent of wearing a lab coat to dinner. The answer is not one clock. It is the stack.

Wilder learns this after a job lead slips away in his inbox. He wants to call himself careless and be done with it. Samantha asks what happened. The message arrived during a crowded handoff. His phone showed several alerts. He had slept badly. The lead mattered, but the system around the moment made the miss more likely. That does not hand him an excuse. It shows where repair can start: fewer alerts during handoffs, a visible place for open loops, and a check before the laptop closes.

Prevention starts where the last second has not yet arrived. If a bad act is most visible at the end, the useful changes often sit earlier. Change training. Change cues. Change the room. Change the cost of asking for help. Change what the group rewards. Last-second scolding is often too late for the body that has already been loaded.

Still, there is a situation that calls for the opposite move. When someone is about to be hurt, do not pause to draw the whole clock map. Stop the harm first. Pull the person back, lock the door, call for help, or say the blunt sentence. The layered account belongs after safety is held. Analysis should make action smarter, not slower when danger is still unfolding.

What to do: Megan admits the edge of her own read, then adds rank, stress, and long observation to the note. She models expertise as better patience.

Why it matters: The strongest person in the scene does not win by sounding certain. The admission protects the reader from making one true clue do all the work.

### Example 4: Jammed Holster Guess
Tags: trigger, prediction, context
The holster strap sticks on the range equipment bench, and range lead Lloyd tugs it free before the review can continue. "The finger went to the trigger too cleanly. That looks deliberate." The next angle breaks the guess. The weapon response happened in milliseconds after the same draw drill in the training history. Lloyd says, "I know the range, and I still guessed too late in the chain."

What to do: Lloyd revises the review from intent-first to chain-first. He marks the motion, the cue, and the practiced response before judging the trainee's choice.

Why it matters: The reveal trains a better instinct. What looks deliberate may still be shaped by a fast cue and a slow habit meeting in one motion.

### Example 6: Binocular Reset
Tags: Kenya, reset, fieldwork
Field assistant Stephane lowers the binocular strap halfway to his chest. The lead observer says, "Read that line back." He has written, "Low rank caused the chase." The olive baboons still move below the Kenya ridge. Stephane stops the routine, crosses out "caused," and says, "Rank raised the odds. I need stress signs and the fieldwork history." The lead observer nods. "Restart there."

What to do: Stephane pauses the habit of writing one-cause notes. He restarts with rank, stress, and years of fieldwork as separate layers.

Why it matters: The pause is the technique. The reader learns to interrupt a tidy cause before it hardens into a false explanation.
